name: Pidgin French
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Nguyễn Đăng Liêm. 1979. Cases and verbs in Pidgin French (Tay Boi) in Vietnam. In P. Mühlhäusler et al. (eds.), Papers in Pidgin and Creole Linguistics No. 2 (Pacific Linguistics A-57), 217-246. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics, Australian National University. DOI 10.15144/PL-A57.217 (ANU Open Research, CC BY-SA 4.0).
catalog_quote: PF uses all the five VN tones. There is a definite correlation between a syllable and a tone, i.e. given a syllable, a certain tone is attached to it, and this depends upon the shape of the syllable (i.e. initial consonant, vowel, and particularly final consonant). This phenomenon of attaching VN tones to intonation languages by the Vietnamese is found also in English spoken by Vietnamese (Liem 1970b: 174-8). The attachment of VN tones to PF syllables follows one of the following rules: Rule 1: PF syllables that are derived from SF syllables ending with -ns and followed by another syllable or other syllables are pronounced with VN mid-rising tone. Rule 2: Syllables in PF ending with a voiceless final stop carry a VN low-rising tone if they are derived from SF syllables ending with -rC(onsonant), and carry a VN high-rising tone if they are derived from SF syllables ending with other consonants or consonant clusters than -rC. Rule 3: Syllables having a front vowel are usually pronounced with VN high-level tone. Sometimes, they are pronounced with VN low-level tone. ... Rule 4: Syllables having a mid-central vowel are pronounced with VN low-level tone. Again, there are exceptions here that should be studied more in depth. Rule 5: Syllables having a schwa off-glide usually carry a VN mid-rising tone when followed by another syllable or other syllables. They are pronounced with VN high-level instead when they are terminal syllables themselves.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Tay Boi (Saigon Pidgin French) is described as tonal: every syllable carries one of the five Saigon Vietnamese tones, assigned predictably by syllable shape (final consonant type, vowel quality, schwa off-glide, and whether the syllable is final or followed by another). Nothing is said about word stress at all; the French stress pattern is not mentioned.
new_statements.exceptions: Rules 3 and 4 have unexplained exceptions ('Sometimes, they are pronounced with VN low-level tone. More statistical research is needed..'; 'Again, there are exceptions here that should be studied more in depth', pp. 222-223).
new_statements.domain_note: Syllable-level tone in the pidgin as spoken by Vietnamese in Saigon (author's own hearing, 1940s-50s); the tone rules refer to syllables 'followed by another syllable' vs 'terminal syllables', i.e. word-internal position, but no word-stress domain is discussed. Intonation (falling-rising) is mentioned only for imperatives (p. 238-239). Schuchardt 1888: 10 [234] adds that Annamese 'Betonungsweisen' seem partly to transfer to the French.
new_statements.identity_note: Tay Boi = tayb1240 (ISO tas), the extinct French-lexified pidgin of Vietnam. Nguyen 1979 describes the Saigon pidgin he heard in the 1940s-50s (Southern/Saigon Vietnamese substrate tones); Schuchardt 1888 describes the Saigon 'Annamito-French' jargon from correspondents' data of 1882-83. Same variety, no dialect ambiguity; the earlier scan's named source (Reinecke 1971) remains unopened.

sources.note: Nothing on stress/accent (a full-text search for stress/accent full text: no 'stress', 'accent'). §1 Phonology pp. 218-223: consonants, vowels, and §1.3 Tones (pp. 222-223): 'PF uses all the five VN tones'; a given syllable carries a fixed Saigon-Vietnamese tone determined by syllable shape (five rules); phonology section explicitly 'supplements' Reinecke 1971: 48-50.
Nothing on stress; reports five Southern Vietnamese tones, citing Nguyen Dang Liem (ANU, pp. 219-242).

sources.citation: Schuchardt, Hugo. 1888. Kreolische Studien VIII: Ueber das Annamito-Französische. Sitzungsberichte der phil.-hist. Classe der kais. Akademie der Wissenschaften (Wien) 116, 227-234 (offprint Wien: Tempsky, 14 pp.)
sources.note: One parenthetical remark, offprint p. 10 (= Sitzungsberichte p. 234): 'An lautlichen Erscheinungen fehlt es keineswegs (es scheinen auch die annamitischen Betonungsweisen zum Theil auf das Französische überzugehen), aber sie sind auf dieser Stufe noch von geringerem Interesse' — i.e. the Annamese accentuation/tone patterns seem partly to carry over to the French; no rule, no data on stress placement.
